uttarā.notes: DN 14 names Koṇāgamana’s birth mother. The packet lacks entries for the yakkhinī’s daughter in SN 10.7 and the two elders of Thig 1.15 and 7.1. AN 8.91–117 lists both a bare Uttarā and Uttarā Nandamātā. The epithet identifies 04 at its occurrence, but a single pick would also apply it to the earlier woman. AN 1.262 gives Nandamātā’s full name as the compound uttarānandamātā. AN 8.89–90 concern monastic procedures. Thag 17.3 leaves the addressee of Ānanda’s verses unnamed. Only the commentary supplies the identification in 03 and even DPPN gives an alternative. AN 8.8, DN 23, MN 91 and MN 152 have men named Uttara. SN 42.13 has a town and the north bank of the Ganges.

uttiya.notes: AN 10.95 identifies the wanderer. DPPN only conjectures that he became the elder in 01. SN 45.30 and 47.16 give the two teachings recounted in 01. The surrounding page hits SN 45.29, 45.31, 47.15 and 47.17 concern other subjects. Thag 1.51 is Godhika’s verse, the first in the group of four companions. Uttiya speaks at 1.54. The chapter recaps in SN 47.20, Thag 1.60 and Thag 1.100 point back to SN 47.16, Thag 1.54 and Thag 1.99 respectively.

uṇṇābha.notes: SN 48.42 is the brahmin’s conversation with the Buddha about the faculties. SN 51.15 gives the exchange with Ānanda at Kosambī. DPPN itself leaves open whether both visitors were the same man. SN 48.41 is the preceding discourse on aging. SN 48.50 and 51.20 mention Uṇṇābha in their chapter recaps.

vacchagotta.notes: MN 73 follows the wanderer through ordination to arahantship, and 01 explicitly names his Thag 1.112 verse. Thag 1.120 names that elder in the chapter recap. AN 3.57 is the question on gifts described in DPPN’s cross-reference to the Vacchagotta Sutta (AN i 160). AN 3.63 identifies the brahmin of Venāgapura by his village and his question about luxurious beds. DPPN only suggests he may be the same wanderer. Its references in 02 to MN 71–73 and SN 33.1 illustrate the travels of 01. The discourse on the three knowledges is MN 71. AN 3.62, MN 70, SN 32.56–57 and SN 44.6 are adjacent page hits.

vajirā.notes: SN 5.10 has the nun and the chariot simile. The Pāli calls the forest Andhavana, spelled Adhavana in DPPN. SN 5.8 and 5.9 feature Sīsupacālā and Selā respectively. The matched word vajiraṁ in MN 35 is the iron thunderbolt held by Vajirapāṇī.

vajjiputta.notes: The candidate is a title entry for the Vajjiputta or Vesāli Sutta. It points to a separate person entry for Vajjiputta (1). SN 9.9 gives the discontented Vajjian monk’s verse and the deity’s reply, echoed in Thag 1.62. Its opening calls him vajjiputtako. Thag 1.119 attributes a different verse to the second elder. The chapter recaps at Thag 1.70 and 1.120 also list the respective monks. SN 9.7 and 9.8 are neighboring discourses.

vajjiyamāhita.notes: In AN 10.94 the householder leaves Campā (campāya nikkhami). The English at 1.2 says Sāvatthī, despite the Campā setting at 1.1. AN 10.93 features Anāthapiṇḍika. The list at AN 6.120–139:1.16 reads vijayamāhiko, rendered Vijayamāhita, a spelling to check against DPPN’s parallel. AN 6.119 and 6.140 are adjacent texts.

vajjī.notes: The entry covers the territory in AN 4.1 and the people in AN 5.58. The travel itinerary is in SN 55.6, one discourse after SN 55.5. The reference in SN 35.87 is in the compound vajjigāmo.

vakkali.notes: AN 1.208 names Vakkalī as foremost in faith. The later AN ranges returned by the citation miss this line. SN 22.87 recounts the visit to the sick monk, while SN 22.86 features Anurādha. Iti 92 gives a parallel teaching without naming Vakkali and Iti 93 concerns fire. Thag 5.8 is his poem, with the attribution written Vakkalitthero in one word.

valāhaka.notes: DN 17:1.13.2 names Mahāsudassana’s royal horse valāhako. SN 22.96:4.6 names the horse ridden by the former king of Kusāvatī. MN 129:37.2 uses valāhako nāma assarājā for a wheel-turning king’s horse in general. All three have the tappable form valāhako, rendered Thundercloud in English, and the packet reports zero mentions. MN 129 describes an individual horse bearing the name. The family of horses asserted in 01 lacks a corresponding passage here.

vappa.notes: AN 4.195 identifies the Sakyan as a disciple of the Jains visiting Mahāmoggallāna. AN 4.194 concerns the Koliyans of Sāpūga. Thag 1.61 has the elder’s attribution. Thag 1.70:2.1 also names him in the chapter recap, outside the packet’s list.

varadhara.notes: The riverside list of wanderers is in AN 4.30 and AN 4.185. The citation also lands on AN 4.28 and 4.29, neither of which names him.

varaṇā.notes: Within AN 2.32–41 the meeting with Ārāmadaṇḍa is at AN 2.37 in this edition. AN 2.38, given in the DPD hint, is set at Madhurā. At AN 2.37:1.2 the Pāli reads bhaddasāritīre, while the English and DPPN call the water Kaddama.

varuṇa.notes: DN 13 invokes the individual god. DN 32 names him among the yakkha chiefs and SN 11.3 identifies him by his banner. The two DN 20 matches are plural Varuṇā, the group covered under varuṇā.

vasabha.notes: Thag 2.10 attributes the two verses to Vasabha. DPPN gives differing accounts of his origins at Vesālī and Sāvatthī. The poem gives no birthplace.

vassakāra.notes: DN 16:1.26.1 names both Sunidha and Vassakāra as the ministers fortifying Pāṭaligāma, contrary to DPPN’s claim that the Dīgha account omits Sunidha. Ud 8.6:15.1 has them together in the compound sunidhavassakārā.

vatrabhū.notes: In SN 2.3 the Buddha addresses Māgha as vatrabhū. DPD and DPPN give the traditional identification with Sakka. SN 2.4 and 2.5 have different speakers and neither contains the epithet.

vaḍḍha.notes: Vaḍḍha credits his mother’s advice in Thag 5.5, and she addresses him by name in Thig 9.1. DPPN counts six verses in Thag 335–339. The poem contains five.
